> **▶ [Solve it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/questions/validate-playlist-sequence)** — free, no card: a runnable editor, the sample and hidden tests, a judged verdict, and the reference solution.

## Problem

A music streaming platform wants to analyze user listening sessions to tell apart two playback modes: **Shuffle Mode** and **Random Mode**. Your job is to decide whether a given listening history could have been produced by **Shuffle Mode**.

The modes are defined as follows:
- **Random Mode**: Each next track is picked uniformly at random from the entire catalog. The same song can appear back-to-back or at any interval.
- **Shuffle Mode**: The system builds a random ordering (a permutation) of every distinct song in the library. It plays through this ordering sequentially. After every song has been played exactly once, it generates a fresh random permutation and continues.

You are provided with `allSongs`, an array containing every unique track in the library, and `playlist`, the sequence of songs a user actually heard. You may assume the user could have started listening partway through a permutation and stopped at any point.

Return `true` if the `playlist` sequence could be a contiguous subsequence taken from a **Shuffle Mode** session; otherwise, return `false`.

## Constraints

- 1 ≤ `allSongs.length` ≤ 100
- 1 ≤ `playlist.length` ≤ 100
- Every element in `allSongs` is a unique, non-empty string.
- Every element in `playlist` exists in `allSongs`.

## Examples

**Example 1**

> **Input:** allSongs = ["A", "B", "C"], playlist = ["A", "B", "C", "A", "C", "B"]
> **Output:** true
> **Explanation:** The listening history can be split into two complete, valid permutations:
> - The first segment, `["A", "B", "C"]`, contains each distinct song exactly once.
> - The second segment, `["A", "C", "B"]`, is another valid permutation.
>
> Since the entire sequence follows the rules of shuffle mode, the result is true.

**Example 2**

> **Input:** allSongs = ["A", "B", "C"], playlist = ["A", "B", "C", "C"]
> **Output:** true

**Example 3**

> **Input:** allSongs = ["A", "B", "C"], playlist = ["A", "B", "C", "C", "C"]
> **Output:** false

## Hints

<details>
<summary>Hint 1</summary>

In Shuffle Mode, the next track is chosen uniformly from all tracks that have not been played yet, so the sequence must be a permutation of a subset of the catalog without repeats until the subset is exhausted.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2</summary>

To validate, simulate the process: maintain a set of played tracks and a pool of candidates, when a track repeats before all candidates are played, it's not Shuffle Mode.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3</summary>

The key edge case is when the sequence ends before all tracks are played, Shuffle Mode allows stopping at any point, but repeats are only allowed after a full cycle.

</details>
